note: Both passages describe God choosing His people before creation, with the aim of shaping them to be like Jesus and adopting them into His family.
Jeremiah was known and set apart by God before birth. Paul extends that idea of being known in advance to every believer.
Paul presents God as working all things by His own plan, and that plan includes the people He has chosen in Christ.
Salvation is traced back to God’s purpose and grace in Christ from before time, rather than to human effort.
Peter says Christ was known before creation. The rescue plan was in place from the start.
Revelation speaks of names written in the Lamb’s book of life, a plan rooted in eternity.
Paul points to God knowing His own people as the firm foundation beneath faith.
Peter brings together God’s foreknowledge, the Spirit’s work and obedience to Jesus in the life of believers.
Paul describes a wisdom God planned before the ages for our glory, the same destination Romans 8 traces.
As people share Adam’s likeness now, believers will share Christ’s likeness. That is the meaning of being conformed to His image.
Colossians calls Jesus the image of God and the firstborn. Romans says believers are being formed into that image as His family.
A chapter later Paul again speaks of people prepared beforehand for glory.
John looks ahead to the day believers will be like Jesus, the end point of being conformed to His image.
Paul describes believers being gradually transformed into the Lord’s likeness by the Spirit.
Both passages present God’s plans as higher than human plans and good for His people, inviting trust when the way is unclear.
The psalm celebrates the permanence of the Lord’s plans. Jeremiah applies that permanence to a promise of good for exiles.
Micah notes that the nations cannot see God’s plan. Jeremiah reassures God’s people that His plan is for their good.
David marvels that God’s plans for His people are beyond counting. Jeremiah says they lead to a hopeful future.
Job affirms that nothing can stop God from carrying out His purpose, which is why His good plans are dependable.
Both were written into the pain of exile. Waiting patiently on God makes sense because He has a future for His people.
Isaiah presents God as knowing the end from the beginning and bringing His purposes to pass.
Ezekiel pictures God personally searching for and gathering His scattered flock, another view of the good future He has planned.
Peter promises that after a season of suffering God will restore and strengthen His people. Suffering is not the final word.
James promises a reward to those who love God and endure trials, showing hardship being worked toward good.
Joseph’s story is the classic picture of Romans 8:28. His brothers intended harm, yet God used it to save many lives.
Paul traces how suffering produces endurance, character and hope. God uses hard things for good.
Both passages speak of the good God has prepared for those who love Him.
Both psalms say that schemes against God and His people do not succeed.
Job’s friend describes God frustrating the plans of the crafty, the same theme as the psalm.
Paul’s confidence rests on the kind of promise God gave Israel through Isaiah: His presence, strength and help in place of fear.
Paul learned that Christ’s power shows up most clearly in weakness. His strength is grace, not self-confidence.
Paul prays for believers to receive God’s power so they can endure with patience.
Paul calls believers to find their strength in the Lord rather than in themselves.
Isaiah describes God giving strength to the weary and renewing those who hope in Him.
Paul prays for inner strength through the Spirit, the source of the strength he speaks of in Philippians.
Jesus links a fruitful life with remaining in Him and His words.
Paul says his adequacy for ministry comes from God, not from himself.
Jesus teaches that fruit comes only from staying connected to Him, like a branch to a vine.
Isaiah names the Lord alone as the source of righteousness and strength.
God gave Joshua the same reassurance He gives Israel in Isaiah: no need to fear, because He is present.
God tells Israel they need not fear because He made them, redeemed them and will be with them through every danger.
Paul states the confidence behind Isaiah’s promise: with God on our side, no opposition can win.
Moses urges Israel to be courageous because God will never abandon them.
The chapter before promises strength for the weary.
A few verses later God repeats the promise, picturing Himself holding His people’s hand.
Paul found God’s grace sufficient and His power evident in weakness.
David’s confidence that God is his light and salvation removes his fear.
The psalm uses the same picture of God’s right hand holding up the one who clings to Him.
Judah is told not to fear a great army because the Lord is with them and will win the battle.
Hebrews quotes Psalm 118 about the Lord as helper, which removes the fear of what people can do.
God’s help is the reason for courage in both passages.
Paul echoes the psalm’s confidence that with the Lord on our side, human opposition loses its power.
Both use the image of one person routing a thousand, possible only because the Lord fights for His people.
God promised that a few faithful Israelites would defeat far larger forces.
Moses told Israel not to fear their enemies because the Lord would fight for them.
At the Red Sea Moses told Israel the Lord would fight for them. Joshua reminds them the same God still does.
David asks God to take up his cause against those attacking him.
Before battle Israel was reminded that the Lord goes with them to fight and to save.
God being on His people’s side is why the few can stand against the many.
The psalm celebrates God’s presence with His people as their fortress.
Earlier in the same speech Joshua reminds Israel that every victory was the Lord’s doing.
God promised Jacob His presence and protection wherever he went. Joshua receives the same promise.
Paul’s call to courage and strength echoes God’s charge to Joshua.
Both call believers to stand firm, stay alert and rely on what God provides.
Both prophets look ahead to God pouring out His Spirit on His people and their children.
At Pentecost Peter explains that the promised outpouring of the Spirit has arrived.
God makes a covenant promise that His Spirit will stay with His people and their descendants.
Jesus invites the thirsty to come to Him, and John explains He meant the Spirit.
Wisdom offers to pour out her spirit on those who turn back, using similar language.
In the new creation God gives the water of life freely to the thirsty.
Zechariah foresees God pouring out a spirit of grace and prayer on His people.
Peter says the promise of the Spirit reaches the next generation too, matching Isaiah’s mention of offspring.
Ezekiel ends a restoration promise with God pouring out His Spirit and no longer hiding His face.
Isaiah uses the same picture elsewhere: when the Spirit is poured out, barren land becomes fruitful.
The Spirit is poured out on Gentiles at Cornelius' house, showing the promise reaches every nation.
Paul describes salvation as renewal by the Holy Spirit, given generously through Jesus.
The psalm pictures God turning desert into springs, the same image of renewal.
Both describe a new covenant in which God’s word and Spirit live within His people.
Hebrews says this new covenant has come through Jesus.
Both contrast fear with the Spirit God gives, a Spirit of power, love and adoption as His children.
Both point to the giving of God’s Son, for people who did not deserve it, as the proof of God’s love.
John returns to the same truth in his letter: God showed His love by sending His only Son so that we could live.
The verse before says the same thing using the picture of the Son of Man being lifted up.
Paul reasons that a God who gave His own Son will not hold back anything else we need.
At Lazarus' tomb Jesus presents Himself as the source of resurrection life for all who believe.
Jesus says the Father’s will is eternal life and resurrection for everyone who believes in the Son.
The chapter closes by repeating the link between believing in the Son and eternal life.
John teaches that our love is a response to God loving us first.
Jesus promises eternal life to His sheep and security that no one can take away.
Paul summarizes the gospel as Jesus coming to save sinners, and counts himself among them.
Paul says God reconciled us through His Son’s death while we were still opposed to Him.
Peter tells the religious leaders that salvation comes through Jesus alone, matching Jesus' own claim.
Jesus also calls Himself the door, the way in to safety and life.
Paul says that through Jesus all believers can approach the Father by the Spirit.
John deliberately opens his Gospel the way Genesis opens, presenting the Word as present and active at creation.
Hebrews says faith understands the universe as made at God’s command.
Paul applies Isaiah’s promise, that those who trust God will not be disgraced, to everyone who believes.
The psalm makes the same promise: hope in the Lord does not end in shame.
Isaiah again promises that God will take away the shame and disgrace of His people.
Hebrews shows that the new covenant includes God choosing not to hold sins against His people, as Isaiah promised.
Micah marvels at a God who pardons sin and delights in mercy, the same God who speaks in Isaiah.
Hebrews repeats that under the new covenant God no longer remembers forgiven sins.
Jeremiah’s new covenant promise includes full forgiveness and sins no longer remembered.
Isaiah uses the picture of deep red stains made clean to describe God’s forgiveness.
Isaiah pictures sin being swept away like a passing cloud and calls God’s people to return.
Both call believers away from the patterns and desires of their old life.
Paul describes the change as removing the old self, having the mind renewed and putting on the new self.
Being a new creation in Christ is the reason the mind is renewed.
Paul says the new self keeps being renewed to reflect its Creator.
John also warns against loving the world’s passing values and points to lasting life in doing God’s will.
Ezekiel promised a new heart and spirit. Paul says that newness becomes real in Christ.
The new creation shows itself in leaving the old self behind and taking up the new.
Isaiah tells Israel to look for the new thing God is doing. Paul says that newness has arrived in Christ.
Both describe God placing His law and Spirit inside His people, giving them a new heart.
Hebrews quotes Jeremiah’s new covenant promise at length.
Paul assures believers that the faithful God who called them will finish His work in them.
A chapter later Paul explains why: God Himself is at work in believers, shaping both desire and action.
Hebrews closes with a prayer that God would equip believers for everything He calls them to do.
Paul says that those who belong to Christ have put their old sinful nature to death with Him.
Jesus teaches that words and actions flow from what is stored in the heart, which is why the heart needs guarding.
Jesus says speech reveals what fills a person’s heart.
Jesus explains that sin starts inside a person rather than coming from outside.
David invites God to examine his heart, a key part of guarding it.
Proverbs links careful speech with a protected life, a close cousin of guarding the heart.
Jeremiah warns how deceptive the human heart can be, which is why it needs watching.
Jesus lists the evil that comes from the heart.
Another proverb urges the listener to keep their heart on the right path.
Proverbs warns against relying on your own heart, which is why wisdom must guide it.
In Gethsemane Jesus urges watchfulness and prayer against temptation, because good intentions are not enough.
James traces temptation back to our own desires. Guarding the heart stops sin early.
Both call for handing your plans and path over to the Lord in trust.
Jeremiah pictures the person who trusts God as a well-watered tree that keeps bearing fruit.
Proverbs contrasts the folly of relying on your own mind with the safety of walking in wisdom.
The psalm joins trusting God with doing what is good.
The psalm invites people to trust God at all times and pour out their hearts to Him.
Isaiah promises deep peace to those whose minds rest on God in trust.
Isaiah’s song turns trust in God as Saviour into freedom from fear.
The psalm counsels quiet patience before the Lord instead of anxious fretting.
Two verses later the same passage warns against being wise in your own eyes.
Both connect entrusting your work to the Lord with seeing your plans established.
Instead of anxiety, both passages point to bringing everything to God in trust.
Peter, like Paul, tells believers to hand their worries to God because He cares.
Jesus teaches His followers not to worry about daily needs because the Father knows and provides.
The psalm invites people to hand their burdens to the Lord, who will hold them up.
Peter draws on the psalm’s picture of throwing your burdens onto the Lord.
Both passages encourage persistent, believing prayer.
Jesus promises that the Father answers prayer offered in His name.
Jesus links faith-filled prayer with receiving from God.
Matthew records Jesus encouraging confident prayer on two separate occasions.
David tells Solomon, and Jeremiah tells the exiles, that God is found by those who seek Him wholeheartedly.
Lamentations calls the people to examine themselves and return to God, the response God asks for in Chronicles.
James also calls for humble repentance and promises that God lifts up the humble.
Isaiah urges people to seek God and turn from wrong, promising generous pardon.
Finding joy in God, and remaining in Jesus, both reshape our desires and lead to answered prayer.
Another psalm says God fulfils the desires of those who revere Him.
Lamentations agrees that God is good to those who wait for Him.
Paul says that even as the body weakens, believers are renewed inwardly day by day.
The psalm uses the same eagle image for God renewing strength.
Both describe God personally teaching and guiding His people on the right path.
Both psalms picture God as a hiding place and shelter for those who trust Him.
Luke records the same teaching about putting God’s kingdom first and trusting Him for the rest.
Jesus promises satisfaction to those who long for righteousness.
Jesus urges people to pursue what lasts forever rather than what spoils.
The psalm says those who revere and seek the Lord will not lack what is good.
Jesus promises that whatever is given up for His sake is repaid many times over.
The psalm says God does not hold back good things from those who live with integrity.
David’s confidence in the Shepherd’s provision matches Paul’s assurance that God will meet every need.
Jesus calls Himself the good shepherd, identifying Himself with the Shepherd of Psalm 23.
Isaiah pictures God tending His flock and carrying the lambs close.
Jesus describes His sheep knowing His voice, following Him and receiving eternal life.
Both describe God giving abundantly, beyond what is asked, so that believers can do good.
Ecclesiastes encourages constant sowing. Paul adds that God supplies the seed and the harvest.
Isaiah also pictures God providing seed for sowing and bread for eating.
Isaiah contrasts fading grass and flowers with God’s lasting word. Jesus claims that same permanence for His own words.
Peter quotes Isaiah on the lasting nature of the Lord’s word.
Balaam’s oracle says God does not lie or change His mind. What He says, He does.
Isaiah says God’s word always accomplishes the purpose for which He sends it.
Jesus also teaches that not the smallest detail of the law will fail before all is fulfilled.
Jesus answers the tempter by quoting Deuteronomy on living by God’s word, not bread alone.
John is told to eat a scroll, a vivid picture of fully taking in God’s message, just as Jeremiah describes eating God’s words.
Ezekiel eats a scroll that tastes sweet. All three prophets picture God’s word being taken in deeply.
The psalmist describes God’s words as sweeter than honey.
Job valued God’s words above his daily food.
The psalm rates God’s word above gold and honey.
Paul says Scripture was written to teach us and to give endurance and hope.
Moses tells parents to pass God’s words on to their children in everyday life.
Samuel and Hosea both teach that God values faithful love and obedience above ritual sacrifice.
David recognizes that God wants a humble, repentant heart more than offerings.
Proverbs says doing what is right pleases God more than sacrifice.
Amos records God rejecting empty religious festivals and calling for justice and righteousness instead.
A scribe agrees with Jesus that loving God and neighbor outweighs every offering.
Jesus quotes Hosea on mercy over sacrifice, which restates Samuel’s point.
Micah sums up what God asks: justice, mercy and a humble walk with Him.
Mark records the same moment, when Jesus explains He came for sinners.
John teaches that keeping Jesus' commands is how we show we truly know and love Him.
John links love for God with keeping His commands, which he says are not a heavy burden.
A few verses later Jesus repeats the link between loving Him and keeping His word.
John defines love as living by God’s commands.
Both encourage believers to keep going in doing good because the work is not wasted.
King Asa is urged to stay strong and keep working because faithfulness will be rewarded.
Paul gives the same encouragement not to tire of doing right.
Paul describes the Christian life as guided by faith rather than by what can be seen.
God’s promise to live among His people reaches its goal in the new creation.
God promised to dwell among Israel at the tabernacle. In Christ, His people themselves become His temple.
Both repeat the heart of the covenant: God belonging to His people and His people belonging to Him.
Paul quotes the promise in Leviticus of God walking among His people.
Jeremiah repeats the covenant promise of God and His people belonging to each other.
Ezekiel foresees an everlasting covenant with God’s sanctuary among His people for good.
Both promise that God will restore His people’s home and fill His house with greater glory than before.
The psalm looks forward to the appointed time for God to show compassion to Zion.
Earlier in the chapter God promises to bring His people back from captivity.
Jesus reads this passage in the Nazareth synagogue and announces that it is fulfilled in Him.
Paul draws on Isaiah to describe the unimaginable good God has prepared for those who love Him.
The psalm also speaks of great goodness God has stored up for those who revere Him.
Both speak of God acting with great goodness for those who wait for Him.
The image of eyes that do not see comes from Isaiah 6. Paul quotes that passage at the close of Acts.
Jesus quotes Isaiah 6 to explain why many hear His teaching without understanding.
Both psalms describe the faithful person refusing the company of the deceitful and wicked.
Being known and loved by God gives strength to people who have little strength of their own.
